Presenters Casey Conaton, Assistant Principal at Smith Middle School, and Chantelle Yancy, Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion & Community Relations, explain the RP continuum, the Fair Process elements of Engagement, Explanation and Expectation Clarity, and the restorative discipline language already embedded in the TSD Student Code of Conduct. The deck cites Michigan Legislature Section 380.1310c, under which restorative practices "should be the first consideration" for offenses such as interpersonal conflicts, bullying, theft, property damage, class disruption and cyberbullying.
2024_201_restorative_practices_presentat.page:
**Item**
Restorative Practices Board Overview — a presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education dated February 6, 2024.

**Presenters**

| Presenter | Role | Restorative training cited |
|---|---|---|
| Casey Conaton | Assistant Principal, Smith Middle School | Foundations in Restorative Practice (2012), Macomb County Intermediate School District training from The Resolution Center; Train the Trainor, Restorative Practices (2022), Troy School District training from IIRP Trainer Bill Boyle |
| Chantelle Yancy | Supervisor, Educational Equity, Inclusion & Community Relations | Restorative Justice Training (2010), Marygrove College Social Justice Program; Foundations in Restorative Practices (2023), Rochester Community Schools |

**Learning Intentions and Outcomes**
Stated goals are gaining knowledge of the principles of RP, learning ways to enact RP in the school environment and why, and discovering ways implementation will impact social change. By the end, participants should be able to explain the model for RP, engage in reflective thinking about personal, student, staff and community lived experiences, and apply the principles of RP. A slide titled "7 Factors to Consider" is included.

**Definition**
Restorative practices is described as a field within the social sciences that studies how to strengthen relationships between individuals as well as social connections within communities. It is presented as a continuum of proactive components supporting strong relationships and safe communities where all members feel they belong, with accountability focused on repairing harm and learning from mistakes. The definition is cited to the International Institute for Restorative Practices at https://www.iirp.edu/restorative-practices/explained.

**Framework — Fair Process ("Do with not to")**
- Engagement: engaging with the individual involved; sharing concern, ideas, problem solving, game planning.
- Explanation: explaining the "why we are here" for the individual.
- Expectation Clarity: whatever the outcome may be, the expectation is clear and understood.
A "Restorative Practices Continuum" slide is also included.

**Rationale**
Schools adopt RP as a "comprehensive way to address disparities in exclusionary discipline i.e., suspensions and expulsions." The approach is framed as proactive and preventative, addressing conflict through collectivity so that harm is repaired through community rather than being confined to two individuals. Restorative justice is presented as an alternative process for accountability and taking responsibility for wrongdoing or harmful actions, ensuring victims or those harmed are heard and are active participants.

**Code of Conduct linkage**
The TSD Student Code of Conduct already states that restorative discipline focuses on the harms, needs and causes of student behavior rather than only rule-breaking and punishment. Students who violate the Code may engage in restorative practices as a consequence, facilitated by school officials, provided the student freely admits wrongdoing and expresses contrition to the offended parties. Listed activities include restitution; alternative suspension including In-School Suspension/Detention; written and verbal apology; participation in diversion programs; community service; outreach and awareness activities; a course of study, book study or other applied learning experience; a behavior plan or behavior contract; counseling in and out of school; engagement with agency and community supports; and student-to-student mediation.

**Practice in schools**
Suite360 modules are used for discipline and restorative measures prior to more severe consequences. Peer conflict resolution has been attempted through circle meetings using reflective questioning ("What happened, what were you thinking? What have you thought about since?"), with ADL learning and apology/restoration between victim and offender. Students have re-entry meetings after major discipline, sometimes including other involved students who are willing to participate. Student-teacher conflicts have been addressed through mutually agreed meetings using the restorative questions. Teachers establish community circles in classrooms to connect academically and non-academically.

**Misconceptions addressed**
That RP does not hold students accountable; that teachers should focus only on academics and not SEL needs; that RP is a one-and-done model; that RP replaces or removes other disciplinary measures, especially for extreme behavior; and that belonging is not essential to RP.

**Legal context**
Michigan Legislature Section 380.1310c is quoted, describing victim-initiated victim-offender conferences approved by the victim's parent or legal guardian, or by the victim directly if the victim is at least age 15.

**Resources**
Restorative Practices Explained; "Do restorative practices work?"; Legal Implications - MI; Klevan, S. (2021), Building a positive school climate through restorative practices, Learning Policy Institute, https://doi.org/10.54300/178.861; and an Improving Student Outcomes interactive worksheet. The deck closes with "Where are We Now?" and "Questions?" slides.
2024_201_restorative_practices_presentat.verbose:
Restorative Practices Board Overview is a slide presentation prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education and dated February 6, 2024. It provides an orientation to Restorative Practices (RP) as a discipline and school-climate framework, connects RP to language already present in the TSD Student Code of Conduct, describes how RP is being used in Troy School District buildings, addresses common misconceptions, and cites the governing Michigan statute.

**Learning Intentions and Outcomes.** The opening slide sets three intentions: gaining knowledge on the principles of RP; learning about ways to enact RP in the school environment and why; and discovering ways that implementation will impact social change. Three outcomes are stated for the end of the session: participants will be able to explain the model for RP; engage in reflective thinking drawing on personal experiences and on student, staff and community lived experiences; and apply the principles of RP. A slide headed "7 Factors to Consider" follows.

**Presenters and their credentials.** Two district staff members present. Casey Conaton is Assistant Principal at Smith Middle School. Her cited experience is Foundations in Restorative Practice (2012), a Macomb County Intermediate School District training delivered by The Resolution Center, and Train the Trainor, Restorative Practices (2022), a Troy School District training delivered by IIRP Trainer Bill Boyle. Chantelle Yancy is Supervisor, Educational Equity, Inclusion & Community Relations. Her cited experience is Restorative Justice Training (2010) through the Marygrove College Social Justice Program, and Foundations in Restorative Practices (2023) through Rochester Community Schools.

**What Restorative Practice is.** The definition slides are cited to the International Institute for Restorative Practices at https://www.iirp.edu/restorative-practices/explained. Restorative practices is defined as a field within the social sciences that studies how to strengthen relationships between individuals as well as social connections within communities. It is characterized as a continuum of proactive components that support setting up strong relationships and safe communities where all members feel they belong, with accountability focused on repairing harm and learning from mistakes.

**Framework: Fair Process.** The framework is summarized by the phrase "Do with not to" and three components. Engagement means engaging with the individual involved, sharing concern and ideas, problem solving and game planning. Explanation means explaining the "why we are here" for the individual. Expectation Clarity means that whatever the outcome may be, the expectation is clear and understood. A separate slide presents the Restorative Practices Continuum.

**Why schools adopt RP.** The presentation states that schools adopt RP as a "comprehensive way to address disparities in exclusionary discipline i.e., suspensions and expulsions," emphasizing proactive and preventative approaches. Conflict is addressed through collectivity, so that harm is addressed through community for repair and the process goes beyond "two individuals." Restorative justice is described as providing an alternative process to accountability and to taking responsibility for wrongdoing and harmful actions, while ensuring victims or those harmed are heard and are active participants in the RJ/RP processes.

**Application to student discipline: the TSD Student Code of Conduct.** The deck reproduces the Code of Conduct's restorative discipline section. A major consideration of the Code of Conduct is to identify appropriate disciplinary actions that will bring about positive student behavior. Restorative discipline focuses on the harms, needs and causes of student behavior, not just the breaking of rules and dispensing of punishment; it attempts to provide students an opportunity to be accountable for the harm caused as well as the opportunity to repair the harm. Students are empowered to help resolve conflict and maintain an environment where the work of the school can happen. The stated goal of restorative discipline is to provide students an opportunity to learn to think differently about harm, to deal with conflict in peaceful and creative ways, to address accountability and responsibility, to focus on one another's humanity, and to problem-solve in terms of community and collaboration.

Student violators of the Code of Conduct may have the opportunity to engage in restorative practices as a consequence of their inappropriate behavior, as facilitated by school officials. The Code notes it is important that any student engaging in restorative practices freely admit to any wrongdoing and express contrition for their actions to the offended parties. Restorative practices developed in response to a Code of Conduct violation may include, but are not limited to: restitution; alternative suspension including In-School Suspension/Detention; apology for the offense, both written and verbal; participation in diversion programs; community service activities; outreach and awareness activities; a course of study, book study, or other applied learning experience; a behavior plan or behavior contract; participation in counseling in and out of school; engagement in agency and community supports; and student-to-student mediation.

**What RP looks like in Troy schools.** The presentation lists Suite360 modules used for discipline and restorative practice measures prior to more severe consequences. Peer conflict and resolution work involves resolving issues with teachers and students, with students assisting with discipline through reflections, ADL learning, and apology or restoration between victim and offender. Staff report having tried to resolve peer conflict through circle meetings, with reflective questioning used to help shed light on the why behind incidents — sample questions include "What happened, what were you thinking? What have you thought about since?" Students have re-entry meetings after any major discipline, often with other students involved if those students are willing to participate. In cases of student/teacher conflict, once both parties agree, a meeting is held and the restorative questions are used to help both sides reach a solution and move forward in a positive manner. Teachers also establish community circles in the classroom to connect with students in both academic and nonacademic ways.

**Misconceptions.** Five misconceptions are enumerated: that RP does not hold students or individuals accountable; that teachers should only focus on academics and not social-emotional learning needs; that RP is a one-and-done model or approach; that RP replaces or removes other disciplinary measures, especially with extreme behavior; and that belonging is not essential to RP.

**Example applications.** Two scenarios contrast punitive and restorative handling. Student A was caught vaping in the bathroom: the traditional or punitive response is detention with no reflection, while the restorative response is student learning with an accountable outcome. Students B and C engaged in a fist fight at school: under the traditional or punitive response, students are immediately removed from the school setting and return without an opportunity to repair harm, a re-entry plan, or learning and reflection; under the restorative alternative, the student may be suspended from school with assigned learning about anger, a re-entry meeting, and an opportunity to repair harm to the students or individuals involved.

**Legal implications.** The deck quotes subsection (2) of Michigan Legislature Section 380.1310c. Restorative practices may include victim-offender conferences that are initiated by the victim; that are approved by the victim's parent or legal guardian or, if the victim is at least age 15, by the victim; that are attended voluntarily by the victim, a victim advocate, the offender, members of the school community, and supporters of the victim and the offender; and that provide an opportunity for the offender to accept responsibility for the harm caused to those affected by the misconduct and to participate in setting consequences to repair the harm. The attendees, known as a restorative practices team, may require the pupil to apologize; participate in community service, restoration, or counseling; or pay restitution. The selected consequences are to be incorporated into an agreement that sets time limits for completion and is signed by all participants. The statute provides that restorative practices should be the first consideration to remediate offenses such as interpersonal conflicts, bullying, verbal and physical conflicts, theft, damage to property, class disruption, and harassment and cyberbullying.

**Closing slides and resources.** The presentation includes slides headed "Where are We Now?" and "Questions?" Additional resources listed are Restorative Practices Explained; "Do restorative practices work?"; Legal Implications - MI; Klevan, S. (2021), Building a positive school climate through restorative practices, Learning Policy Institute, https://doi.org/10.54300/178.861; and an Improving Student Outcomes interactive worksheet.
